summary: Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID) helps service providers and security response teams communicate and trace security incidents such as worms, phishing, and denial of service. It defines extensions to IODEF for cooperative handling.

plainLanguage.summary: When an attack comes from somewhere else on the Internet, the team that is being attacked has to ask the other networks to help find where it started. RID is a way of making that request: a signed XML message that can be passed from one provider to the next, each of which adds its own trace information, until the source is found.

subtitle: How the teams that run networks ask each other to help trace and stop an attack.

tldr.problem: When an attack crosses several networks, the teams that could trace or stop it have no standard, secure way to ask each other for help, and email may not be read with the needed urgency.
tldr.mechanism: RID wraps IODEF incident documents in a small XML envelope that names the message type, the destination and the sharing policy. Five message types, Request, Acknowledgement, Result, Report and Query, are signed, optionally encrypted, and passed between peers.
tldr.outcome: RID obsoletes RFC 6045, which moves to Historic status. This version is a Standards Track document, while RFC 6045 was Informational.

sections.title: What RID Is For
sections.content:
Organizations need help from other parties to identify incidents, mitigate malicious activity targeting their computing resources, and to gain insight into potential threats through the sharing of information. That coordination might entail working with a service provider to filter attack traffic, working with a service provider to resolve a configuration issue that is unintentionally causing problems, contacting a remote site to take down a bot network, or sharing watch-lists of known malicious IP addresses in a consortium. The term "service provider" is used for any type of service provider or Computer Security Incident Response Team that may be involved in RID communications.

Incident handling involves the detection, reporting, identification and mitigation of an incident, whether it is a benign configuration issue, an IT incident, an infraction to a service level agreement, a system compromise, a socially engineered phishing attack, or a denial-of-service attack. When an incident is detected, the response may include filing a report, notifying the source of the incident, asking a service provider for resolution or mitigation, or asking for the source to be located. One of the more difficult cases is the one in which the source of an attack is unknown, which requires the ability to trace the attack traffic iteratively upstream through the network so that further action can be taken. Where accurate records of an active session between the target and the source are available, the source is easy to identify.

Real-time inter-network defense outlines a proactive method of communication between networks that shares incident-handling data while integrating existing detection, tracing, source identification and mitigation mechanisms. RID provides a secure method to communicate incident information, enabling the exchange of Incident Object Description and Exchange Format (IODEF) XML documents. It considers the security, policy and privacy issues of exchanging potentially sensitive information, and includes provisions for confidentiality, integrity and authentication.

The data in RID messages is represented in an XML document using IODEF and RID. By following that model, integration with other parts of incident handling is simplified. Methods are built into the communication system to indicate what actions need to be taken closest to the source in order to halt or mitigate the effects of the incident. RID is intended to work with a variety of existing and possible future detection, tracing and response approaches, and incidents may be extended to include information technology incidents, where RID enables communication between or within providers for non-security IT incidents.

Coordinating with other teams is not strictly a technical problem. There are procedural, trust and legal considerations that might stop an organization from sharing information, so RID provides information and options that organizations then apply their own policies to. Organizations must develop policies and procedures for the use of the RID protocol and IODEF.
sections.plainLanguage: When an attack comes from somewhere else on the Internet, the team that is being attacked has to ask the other networks to help find where it started. RID is a way of making that request: a signed XML message that can be passed from one provider to the next, each of which adds its own trace information, until the source is found.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 6045
sections.content:
The document lists the changes from its predecessor. This document is on the Standards Track, while RFC 6045 was published as Informational, and it obsoletes RFC 6045 and moves it to Historic status. It refers to the updated RID transport specification, RFC 6546, where appropriate.

The edits are primarily improvements to the informational descriptions. The descriptions now make clear that IODEF and RID can be used for all types of incidents and are not limited to network security incidents. The language moves the focus from attacks to incidents where appropriate, and the term "network provider" is replaced with the more generic "service provider". Several introductory informational sections have been removed as they are not necessary for implementing the protocol.

Sections 1, 2, 3 and 12 provide background information and considerations, while RID systems participating in a consortium are REQUIRED to fully implement Sections 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 to prevent interoperability concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier version of this protocol was an Informational document, describing an idea. This one is a standard, and it replaces the earlier one. Most of the changes are to the wording: the focus moves from attacks to incidents in general, and the term for a network operator becomes the more general "service provider".

sections.title: Why Incidents Are Hard to Trace
sections.content:
An incident may be a benign configuration issue, an IT incident, an infraction to a service level agreement, system compromise, a worm or Trojan infection, or a single- or multiple-source denial-of-service attack. The goal of tracing a security incident may be to identify the source or to find a point on the network as close to the origin as possible. RID messages can be communicated between entities to report or investigate any type of incident and allow actions to be taken when the source or a point closer to it is known. Methods to accomplish mitigation may include remediation of a configuration issue, filtering or rate-limiting the traffic close to the source, or taking the host or network offline. Care must also be taken to ensure that the systems involved are not abused, and to use proper analysis in deciding whether attack traffic is in fact attack traffic at each provider involved.

Investigating security incidents is difficult because attackers go to great lengths to obscure their identity. The true source might be identified through an existing connection to the attacker's point of origin, but the attacker may not connect to the compromised system for a long time after the initial compromise, or may reach it through a series of compromised hosts spread across the network. Other methods of obscuring the source include targeting the host with the same attack from multiple sources using both valid and spoofed source addresses, which can compromise a machine and leave the hard task of locating the true origin to the administrators.

Through analysis, these techniques may be grouped into indicators of compromise to be shared via IODEF and RID, which helps improve detection capabilities. Security incidents, including distributed denial-of-service attacks, can be difficult or nearly impossible to trace. Some of the difficulties are that the incident originates from multiple sources; that it may leverage social engineering or other methods that look like legitimate access, such as outbound web sessions from user systems; that the attack may include traffic meant to consume server resources, such as a SYN flood that does not significantly increase bandwidth use; that the traffic may include valid destination services that cannot be blocked because they are essential to the business, such as DNS servers or HTTP requests; that the attack may use varying packet types, including TCP, UDP and ICMP; that it may come from zombies or large botnets, which then require additional searches to find the controlling server; that it may use a very small number of packets from any particular source, making a trace after the fact nearly impossible; and that the indicators of a compromise may be difficult to detect.

If the source cannot be determined from IP address information, it may be possible to trace the traffic on other characteristics, such as increased bandwidth utilization or the type of packets seen by the client. With spoofed source addresses, identifying the source is not a trivial task.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers hide. They may not connect again for months, they may come through a chain of already-compromised machines, they may send a trickle of packets that looks like normal traffic, or they may fake the source address entirely. Those tricks are the reason a trace often has to be repeated network by network, one provider at a time.

sections.title: Communication Topology and Policy
sections.content:
Expediting communication between incident response teams and service providers is essential when an incident crosses network access points between them. Because of the urgency, there must be an effective system in place, involving multiple means of communication to avoid a single point of failure. Email is one way to transfer information about an incident or packet traces, but it may not be received in a timely fashion or acted upon with the same urgency as a phone call or a mechanism like RID.

Each provider maintains its own system capable of communicating via RID and integrates it with a management station used for monitoring and analysis. An alternative for providers lacking sufficient resources is to have a neutral third party with access to the provider's network resources perform the incident-handling functions, for example a central organization acting as the response team for a country or a consortium providing centralized resources.

One goal of RID is to prevent the need to permit access to other networks' equipment. The messaging mechanism may be a logical or physical out-of-band network so that the communication is secure and unaffected by the state of the network under attack. The links would be direct connections, virtual or physical, between peers who have agreed use and abuse policies through a consortium. Consortiums might be linked through policy comparisons and additional agreements to form a larger web of peers, based on regions or logical groups. Contact information and the IP addresses of RID systems must be coordinated between bilateral peers by a consortium, and the security, configuration and confidence rating schemes of the peers must be negotiated to meet the requirements of the fully connected network.

The network used for the communication should consist of out-of-band or protected channels, or encrypted channels dedicated to the transport of RID messages. Use of the communication network and the protocol must be for pre-approved, authorized purposes only, and it is the responsibility of each participating party to follow the guidelines set by the global use policy established through peering agreements or consortium guidelines. The purpose of such policies is to avoid abuse of the system, and the global policy may differ by domain, for example a government network and the Internet would adopt different guidelines. Privacy issues must be considered in public networks.

RID requests must be legitimate incidents and not used for purposes such as sabotage or censorship, for example a request to rate-limit legitimate traffic to stop information being shared between users, or to restrict a competitor's access. The system should be configurable to either require user input or automatically continue traces, which lets a network manager assess the available resources before continuing a request. If the confidence rating provided in IODEF is low, it may not be in the provider's best interest to continue, and requests must be issued by authorized individuals from the initiating team under policy guidelines set through peering or a service level agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: Providers talk to each other over protected links, either out of band so that a broken network cannot stop the conversation, or encrypted. Each pair signs up to rules about what may be shared, and a request must be a real incident rather than a way of harming someone else's traffic.

sections.title: The Five Message Types
sections.content:
The five RID message types MUST be implemented. RID messages use both the IODEF and RID documents, which MUST be encapsulated for transport as specified in RFC 6546, and they are generated and received on designated systems for RID communications. When an application receives a RID message, it must be able to determine the type of message and parse it accordingly. The message type is specified in the RIDPolicy class, which may also be used by the transport protocol.

  • The Request message is used when a request is needed. A Request with options set to 'InvestigationRequest' leverages existing peer relationships to notify the service provider closest to the source that a security-related incident occurred, so that any necessary action can be taken there. A Request set to 'TraceRequest' is used when the traffic has to be traced iteratively through networks to find the source. The 'InvestigationRequest' type is used for all other Request messages.
  • The Acknowledgement message is sent to the initiating RID system from each of the upstream providers to give the status of a Request, and is also used to give the reason why a Request, Report or Query was not accepted.
  • The Result message provides a final report and the notification of actions taken for a Request. It is sent to the initiating team through the network of RID systems in the path of the trace, as notification that the source of the attack was located.
  • The Report message is used to report a security incident for which no action is requested, for example to correlate attack information, share incident information, or gather statistics and trending information.
  • The Query message is used to request information about an incident or incident type from a trusted system communicating via RID, and the response is provided through the Report message.

A Request sent between RID systems to stop traffic at the source requires enough information to enable the administrators to decide about the importance of continuing the trace, the incident or IP packet information needed to carry out the trace or investigation, contact information for the origin of the communication, network path information to help prevent routing loops from perpetuating a trace, and a unique identifier for a single attack, which should be used to correlate traces to multiple sources in a denial-of-service attack. If a RID system receives a TraceRequest that contains its own information in the path, the trace must cease and an alert generated to inform the network operations staff that a tracing loop exists.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five kinds of message. A Request asks for help, an Acknowledgement says whether the request was accepted, a Result reports what was found, a Report just files information, and a Query asks a question that comes back as a Report. A request carries enough for the receiver to judge whether to keep tracing, and it carries the path so a trace cannot loop.

sections.title: The IODEF-RID Schema
sections.content:
Three classes are included in the RID extension to facilitate RID communications. The RequestStatus class indicates the approval status of a Request message, the IncidentSource class reports whether a source was found and identifies the source hosts or networks, and the RIDPolicy class provides information on the agreed policies and specifies the type of communication message being used.

The intent in maintaining a separate schema, rather than using the AdditionalData extension of IODEF, is the flexibility of sending messages between RID hosts. Because a RID message includes both the RID and IODEF documents, it acts as an envelope, so the policy and security defined at the RID message layer apply to both documents. Separating the schemas also allows the RIDPolicy class to be extracted easily for use in the message and by the transport protocol. The RIDPolicy information is not required to be encrypted, so separating it out removes the need to decrypt and parse the IODEF document to decide how a message should be handled at each host.

The RID class has one attribute, a required language code, and may contain three aggregate classes, each optional. RIDPolicy is used by all message types to facilitate policy agreements between peers, consortiums or federations, and to route messages. RequestStatus is used only in Acknowledgement messages, reporting status on a Request or an error with the receipt or processing of a Report, Query or Result message. IncidentSource is used in the Result message only, giving the information on the identified source host or network of a trace or investigation. Each of the three may be the only class present, and RIDPolicy may be the only class when used by the transport protocol, since that information should be as small as possible and may not be encrypted. The RequestStatus message must be able to stand alone without an IODEF document, limiting the data transported to the required elements.

The RIDPolicy class holds a restriction enumeration, the message type, the message destination, and extended versions of both, plus the Node class identifying the RID system, the IncidentID pointing back to the IODEF data model, one or more PolicyRegion values, one or more TrafficType values, and an optional ReportSchema that can embed an IODEF document or XML documents that conform to other schemas. The IncidentID includes the name of the team, an incident number and an instance number, which lets related incidents such as botnets or several hops of compromised systems be grouped. The PolicyRegion values describe the expected sharing range: ClientToSP, SPToClient, IntraConsortium, PeerToPeer, BetweenConsortiums and an escape value.
sections.plainLanguage: A RID message is a small envelope around the incident document. The envelope says what kind of message this is, who it is for, and under which sharing policy it may travel. That way the receiver can decide what to do with a message before it even reads the incident details inside it.

sections.title: What a Request Must Carry
sections.content:
The Request message type is used to request assistance in a computer security investigation. The investigation request may be directed to another party that can assist with forensics and continue the investigation, or to a service provider to trace traffic from an unknown source. A Request set to 'InvestigationRequest' leverages existing bilateral peer relationships in order to notify the provider closest to the source of valid traffic that some event occurred. A Request set to 'TraceRequest' may be sent to an upstream peer to trace back through the network to locate the source of malicious traffic.

The information carried by a Request comes from several data structures. From RID: the RIDPolicy with the message type, the IncidentID and the destination policy information. From IODEF: timestamps for detection, start, end and report; the incident identifier; the confidence rating of the incident, through the Impact and Confidence classes; the System class, listing both source and destination; the Expectation class, used to request specific actions close to the source; path information of nested RID systems, beginning with the originator of the trace, using IODEF EventData with the category set to 'infrastructure'; and the Event, Record and RecordItem classes to include example packets and other information about the incident.

Standards for encryption and digital signatures are used as well. The initiating team signs at least one of the original elements in the RecordItem class with a detached XML digital signature, passed to all systems receiving the Request, and the sending team signs the whole IODEF-RID document with an enveloped signature. XML encryption is applied as required by policy, agreements and data markers.

Security requirements include the ability to encrypt the contents of the Request message using the public key of the destination RID system. The incident number increases whether the request is an InvestigationRequest or a TraceRequest, to keep it unique. Relaying peers append their own Autonomous System or RID system information using the path information, so that the Result can come back the same way and report any actions taken. The request is recorded in the state tables of both the initiating and destination systems, and the destination provider is responsible for any actions taken, in adherence to its service level agreements or policies. It MUST confirm that the traffic actually originated from the suspected system before taking any action, and confirm the reason for the request.

A denial-of-service attack can have many sources, resulting in multiple traces. It may be valid to continue several traces for one attack, and the path information lets administrators see whether a trace has already passed through a network. If a single Request results in divergent paths, a separate instance number must be used under the same IncidentID.
sections.plainLanguage: A request has to carry enough for the next provider to decide whether to act: what happened and when, how sure the sender is, what the traffic looked like, who to contact, and which other providers have already been asked. Each provider that handles it adds its own name to the path, and the answer travels back along that same path.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
RID leverages existing security standards and the data markings in RIDPolicy to achieve the required level of security for the exchange of incident information. The standards used are TLS and the XML security features of encryption and digital signatures. They provide clear methods to ensure that messages are secure, authenticated and authorized, meet policy and privacy guidelines, and maintain integrity. Implementers should refer to the XML Signature Best Practices for guidance on improving security and mitigating attacks.

The originator of a Request MUST use a detached signature to sign at least one of the original elements in the RecordItem class, to provide authentication to all upstream participants in the trace or investigation. Upstream peers may add further RecordItem entries signed by themselves, while keeping the original entries and their detached signatures. The data is signed at the RecordItem level because several RecordItems may exist within an IODEF document and may come from different sources, and exclusive canonicalization is REQUIRED for the detached signature. If a Request includes no RecordItem entry, a timestamp must be used so that there is data to sign for the multi-hop authentication case. For all message types, the full IODEF-RID document MUST be signed with an enveloped signature by the sending peer, and the signature is placed in a Signature element.

The message transport is specified in RFC 6546. The public key infrastructure is used for authentication, and multi-hop request authentication is covered in its own section. Consortiums and public key infrastructures are related: trust levels can be established in cross-certification processes where entities compare PKI policies covering the management and handling of an entity's certificates. Agreements between entities SHOULD also include a common understanding of the use of the RID security, policy and privacy options, and the formality of those agreements should be decided by the entities or consortiums creating them.

Privacy concerns and system use guidelines have their own section, because the incident data carried in RID messages can be sensitive. The security considerations section adds the concerns that apply to the transport, storage and exchange of the information: availability, confidentiality and integrity. Protected tunnels between systems accepting RID communications provide confidentiality, integrity, authenticity and privacy at the transport layer, while encryption and digital signatures at the IODEF document level provide them at the application layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the messages travel between organisations and may contain sensitive details, they are signed, and may be encrypted, at two levels: the incident document itself and the link it travels over. Each organisation also has to agree with its peers, in advance, on the rules for what may be shared and who may see it.

items.title: Request
items.text: Asks for help: a TraceRequest follows the traffic upstream, an InvestigationRequest asks a provider near the source to act.

items.title: Acknowledgement
items.text: Tells the sender the status of a request, or why a request, report or query was not accepted.

items.title: Result
items.text: The final report, sent back along the path of the trace, naming the source and any action taken.

items.title: Report
items.text: Files an incident for which no action is asked, such as shared statistics or trending information.

items.title: Query
items.text: Asks a trusted peer for information about an incident or a type of incident; the answer comes as a Report.

viz.caption: TWO WAYS TO ORGANISE THE WORK

columns: Each provider runs its own RID system
A neutral third party does the work

Providers with the resources to staff incident handling themselves

viz.caption: THE POLICY REGION VALUES IN RIDPolicy

items.label: Client to provider
items.desc: A client asked its service provider; the relationship usually rests on contracts or agreements.

items.label: Provider to client
items.desc: A provider sent a request or report to its client.

items.label: Within a consortium
items.desc: No restrictions within a group that has agreed how the data is shared and protected.

items.label: Peer to peer
items.desc: No restrictions between two peers, but further evaluation may be needed beyond that point.

items.label: Between consortiums
items.desc: No restrictions between consortiums that have agreed use and abuse guidelines.
